p_8c4dc81c955ff498.title: Ode to Weeds
p_8c4dc81c955ff498.standfirst: Three field-guide entries that turn out to be character studies, and an ending that hands back the dignity the word ‘weed’ took away.
paragraphs: The poem is built like a page torn from a botanical key — three species, each given its own heading and its own paragraph of observed behaviour. But the vocabulary is stolen from human judgement rather than botany. Cutgrass is ‘invasive, aggressive’; dogtooth is ‘monogamous’; vetch ‘soldiers’ upward. These are the words we actually use about weeds, and setting them beside real plants exposes how much moral freight we load onto things that are only trying to live.

The argument arrives in three lines at the end: ‘It is enough / to give them elegant names: / Leersia, Cynodon, Lathyrus.’ Enough for what? The poem doesn’t say, and is better for not saying. The Latin is the ode — the act of naming precisely is the praise. That makes this quietly an ars poetica for the whole collection, which returns again and again to binomials as a form of attention.
The risk is that the ending is very light — three lines carrying the weight of twenty-four. A reader in a hurry could take the names as decoration rather than as the poem’s entire claim.

craft.move: A technical noun doing metaphorical work
craft.line: they meticulously erode / the black mortise of asphalt
craft.why: A mortise is a joiner’s slot cut to receive a tenon. Calling the road’s cracks a mortise casts the weed as patient carpentry rather than damage — the plant is finishing a joint the road left open.

craft.move: Three words that reverse the poem’s moral
craft.line: Always first to arrive, / they seek accidents.
craft.why: ‘Seek accidents’ recasts opportunism as something closer to courage or vocation. Once you have read this line, ‘invasive’ two lines later sounds like a slur rather than a description.

craft.line: So they have been labeled: / invasive, aggressive.
craft.why: The passive voice keeps the labeller offstage. Nobody is blamed, which lets the reader notice they are the one doing the labelling.

p_df393f9831fb4730.title: Ode to a Pencil
p_df393f9831fb4730.standfirst: A comic ode in the Neruda line, arguing that the capacity to be wrong is a virtue and the eraser is its emblem.
paragraphs: The poem sets up a straight opposition — pencil against pen, revision against commitment — and then keeps finding new ways to press it. The pen is ‘a dictator’ marching ‘along a black path of no return’; the pencil ‘understand[s] human panic.’ What saves this from being a one-joke poem is that the pencil’s virtue is defined entirely by our failures. It is modest because we are wrong so often.

The best writing is in the small human particulars rather than the grand claims. ‘You know we want to spell definitely / without committing a literary crime’ works because *definitely* is the word people genuinely misspell — the poem has watched someone at a desk, not just thought about pencils. Compare ‘a heart of compressed carbon / dreaming, perhaps, of diamond’, which reaches for the cosmic and lands on a familiar image.

The close earns its aphorism by routing it through a physical fact: sharpening destroys the pencil and renews it at the same time. ‘Perhaps wisdom is simply knowing / how to take a little off the top / and start over’ would be a fortune cookie on its own; after thirty lines of watching the thing grind down, it isn’t.

craft.line: to wear an eraser like a dunce cap / for sins it didn’t commit
craft.why: The eraser is punished for mistakes the writer made — the dunce cap sits on the tool rather than the hand. It is the poem’s thesis compressed into an image before the argument has even begun.

craft.line: the weapon of the tentative, / the scepter of the first draft
craft.why: Weapon and scepter belong to epic; tentative and first draft belong to a kitchen table. The collision is the joke, and it is the collection’s most reliable comic engine.

craft.line: and last night’s math mistake
craft.why: After ‘yesterday’s bad poetry’, the homework brings the poem back down to the actual desk. The pairing quietly admits that poems and long division are the same order of human error.

p_59202c684e2b0a30.title: Ode to Chloroplasts
p_59202c684e2b0a30.standfirst: A poem of debt: photosynthesis as a gift we never acknowledge, ending on the most quietly religious image in the collection.
paragraphs: The poem’s method is exchange. Light in, sugar out; breath in, breath out; ghost given back as promise. Almost every sentence describes a transaction, and the middle section names the theme outright with one of the collection’s recurring mock-liturgical headings — ‘The Debt We Owe:’. That heading device shows up in Chocolate, Coffee, the Mirror and the Refrigerator too, and it is becoming a signature.

The strongest line is the last: ‘weaving them / into the quiet bread of the world.’ *Bread* carries the Eucharist without the poem ever having to mention it, and *quiet* does the real work — the sacrament happens continuously, unannounced, in every leaf. It is a better ending than the poem’s more assertive middle.

The weaker passage is the paired negation — ‘No king ever built a house so small. / No god ever made so much / from so little.’ It is well balanced, but it argues where the rest of the poem shows. The line about the stolen sun does more with less.

craft.line: Yet every bite of fruit is a stolen sun.
craft.why: Recasting eating as theft makes gratitude the only honest response, which is exactly what an ode is for. The word ‘stolen’ also implicates the reader, mid-sentence, without accusation.

craft.move: Industrial diction in a nature poem
craft.line: Your miniature jade factories catch / the falling light
craft.why: ‘Factories’ ought to clash with ‘jade’ and doesn’t — it insists that the machinery of the living world is machinery, and beautiful, and both at once.

craft.line: You do not wait for applause / or ask why the dark is heavy.
craft.why: The poem has spent twenty lines personifying an organelle, then declines to give it the one human trait — self-pity — that would make it sentimental.

p_442db0a626e0e282.title: Ode to Awe
p_442db0a626e0e282.standfirst: An ode to an emotion rather than an object, built on the best grammatical metaphor in the collection.
paragraphs: This is the most rhetorical of the comic odes — it works in blocks, each stanza doing one job. Setup: awe as burglar. Diagnosis: we are small. Trigger: three examples. Break: ‘and snap.’ Release: the walls vanish. That architecture is clear enough to feel almost like an essay, and the poem’s pleasure is in the sentence-level surprises it hangs on that frame.

‘We are accountants of the trivial’ is the diagnosis in five words. But the poem’s finest moment is grammatical: ‘We are no longer nouns walking through a schedule; / we are the weather, the lightning, the shock.’ To be a noun is to be a fixed, nameable thing with a place in a sentence; weather is a process. The metaphor makes a genuine claim about what awe does to the self, and it makes it in the vocabulary of language itself.
One patch of slack: ‘the price of lettuce’ and ‘our credit scores’ are doing the same job in different stanzas, and the second lands softer for arriving after the first.

craft.line: O awe, you sudden burglar of the breath, / who kick the doors of routine off their hinges
craft.why: Awe is usually written as ascent. Framing it as a break-in makes it something that happens *to* you against your will, which sets up the ending’s ‘terrified, magnificent grin.’

craft.line: and snap.
craft.why: After three long, mounting examples the poem stops on a monosyllable and a full stop. The line enacts the thing it describes — the reader’s eye is what breaks.

craft.line: It simply makes the room so infinitely tall / that the walls vanish
craft.why: The walls don’t fall; the room outgrows them. The prison was never locked — the poem’s last claim — and this image gets there before the final line says it.

p_39051a2442538cd2.title: Ode to Cashews
p_39051a2442538cd2.standfirst: Sixty-six words, no waste — the most economical poem here, and a small argument for standing outside the crowd.
paragraphs: The poem opens by defining its subject negatively — not the almond, not the pea — so the cashew arrives already positioned between hardness and blandness. That is efficient characterisation: three lines and the reader can taste it. ‘A soft crunch, / surrendering to velvet’ is the sensory centre, and *surrendering* is the word that turns texture into temperament.

The middle stanza does something the other food odes don’t: it uses a real botanical oddity as structure. The cashew grows outside its fruit, sheathed in a caustic shell. The poem calls this ‘botanic rebellion’ and lets the fact carry the moral, so that the final claim — that it is fine ‘to dangle outside the mainstream’ — feels discovered rather than imposed.
It is the shortest poem in the collection and arguably the tightest. Nothing here is doing decorative work.

craft.line: Neither hard like the almond, / nor plain like the pea
craft.why: The subject is located by what surrounds it before it is described at all — a compression trick that saves the poem ten lines of adjectives.

craft.line: wrapped in toxic armor / to guard a rich, buttery soul
craft.why: Botanically accurate and psychologically loaded in the same breath. The poem never says the cashew is a person, and never needs to.

craft.line: leaving us always / wanting more
craft.why: The last line performs its own content: the poem stops early, and the reader feels the shortage it describes.

p_5b92d9e0ccd4a474.title: Ode to Chocolate
p_5b92d9e0ccd4a474.standfirst: The most exuberant of the consumable odes, and the one that leans hardest on the collection’s mock-liturgical formula.
paragraphs: Two headings — ‘The Liturgy of the Wrapper:’ and ‘The Tao of the Cacao:’ — frame eating a chocolate bar as religious observance. The device is fun and the poem commits to it, but it is worth noticing that this is now the fourth or fifth poem to use a mock-sacred heading. Used once it is a joke; used repeatedly it becomes a habit of mind, and this poem is where a reader may first feel the pattern.

The best writing is in the sound of the opening act. ‘The foil tears back with a crisp, anticipatory snap’ is entirely made of the noise it describes — those hard c and p consonants are the wrapper. ‘Leaving only happy fingerprints and existential peace’ gets its laugh from register collision: fingerprints are forensic and domestic, existential peace is philosophy, and chocolate has produced both.

‘A dark and solid promise of grace under pressure’ is the one phrase that arrives borrowed — Hemingway’s definition of courage, applied to confectionery. The poem is funnier when its comparisons are its own.

craft.line: The foil tears back with a crisp, anticipatory snap.
craft.why: Six plosives in eleven words. The line is audible before it is understood, which is the right order for a poem about anticipation.

craft.line: outlasting empires, awkward first dates, / and the best-laid plans of dietitians everywhere
craft.why: The list descends from world-historical to personal to petty, and the descent is the joke. Burns is glanced at in passing without being leaned on.

craft.line: You merely wait on the counter
craft.why: Every ode in this collection eventually praises its subject for not demanding praise. Here it lands well because a chocolate bar genuinely does just sit there.

p_6078318e4c2382c4.title: Ode to Coffee
p_6078318e4c2382c4.standfirst: The dark twin of the chocolate poem — same structure, entirely different weather, and a refusal to be comforting.
paragraphs: The first line makes the cup a funeral: ‘Dark velvet ghost in a white ceramic shroud.’ From there the poem holds a tone the other consumable odes don’t attempt. Morning is not cheerful here; it is survival. ‘We are all ruins before you touch our lips’ places the reader in a state of collapse before the drink arrives.

The turn that makes the poem is its refusal of the obvious praise: ‘You do not taste like comfort. / You taste like survival and sharp edges.’ An ode that declines the easiest compliment available to it has to find a harder one, and this poem does — ‘A warm, black compass in a directionless room’ — where the warmth is real but the room stays lost.

The last stanza glances at Nietzsche and softens him. ‘We pour you into the void, / and the void sings back in steam’ takes the abyss that gazes back and makes it kindly, domestic, breathing. The final line has no full stop, and whether or not that was deliberate it suits a world that hasn’t finished rekindling.

craft.line: Dead clay becomes a nervous system.
craft.why: Five words covering the entire distance from body-as-earth to body-as-mind. It is also, literally, what caffeine does — the metaphor is a mechanism.

craft.line: A thousand sleeping ants of thought wake up and march.
craft.why: Thought is given a plural, a scale and a direction at once. The slight unpleasantness of ants is right: this is not a comfortable awakening.

craft.line: You are the midnight oil burned at dawn.
craft.why: The idiom is deliberately misused — midnight oil belongs to the night before. It catches exactly the disorientation of a morning that is really the end of a long night.

p_7183cf9a9d6a440a.title: Ode to Red-Winged Blackbirds
p_7183cf9a9d6a440a.standfirst: The most formally daring poem here: an ode staged as an antiphon, with the birds allowed to speak in their own phonemes.
paragraphs: Most of these odes address their subject directly. This one steps back and stages it. After the Latin binomial and a dedication, the poem alternates ‘He:’ and ‘She:’ across four short stanzas, so the layout on the page reproduces the call-and-response of a marsh in April. Form and subject are doing the same thing, which is rare and hard.

The braver choice is letting the birds sing untranslated. ‘terrr-eeee!’, ‘oak-a-lee!’, and the female’s ‘chit, chit, chit, chit, chit, chit, / cheer, teer, teer, teerr’ are transcription, not description. A poem that described the song would keep the human at the centre; this one hands the microphone over. The six repetitions of *chit* also make the female the noisier bird on the page, which is true to life and a nice correction to the male’s flashier plumage.

The ending leaves observation for metaphysics — ‘Reveal, from the wing of now-self, / thrumming wingtips / of hereafter-self.’ It is the poem’s biggest reach and its most exposed moment: after such exact watching, the abstraction may feel like a different poem arriving. The Persephone framing earlier earns some of it, since the whole piece has been arguing that a marsh in spring is a rite.

craft.line: He: / launches from a cattail
craft.why: The alternating speaker tags are borrowed from drama and used as field notation. The poem is scored rather than written.

craft.line: The reedy, procreant edge / of the pond pulses: / oak-a-lee!
craft.why: Three heavy stresses on ‘pond pulses’ then release into the bird’s own syllables. ‘Procreant’ is doing double duty — Whitman’s word, and simply accurate.

craft.line: Persephone herself rouses / the red-winged blackbird, / insisting he signal her return
craft.why: The blackbird’s arrival really is one of the first reliable markers of spring in a northern marsh. The myth is used to explain a fact rather than to dress it up.

p_7b21b8ea262109ed.title: Ode to Reading Glasses
p_7b21b8ea262109ed.standfirst: An ageing poem hidden inside an object ode, and the only one here generous enough to admit that the blur was beautiful too.
paragraphs: The poem never says the word *ageing*, and never needs to. It says ‘the world grew soft at the edge’ and ‘the small print retreating like a shy animal.’ Loss is described entirely as a change in the behaviour of print and light, which keeps the self-pity out and lets the reader supply the years.

Its thesis is the modest middle stanza: ‘You do not cure time. / You only build a tiny, temporary room / where the eye may sit down again.’ *Sit down* is the word that does it — an exhausted verb, granted to an eye. The claim is small and exactly true, and the poem is honest enough not to promise more.

Then the comedy — the hunting, the couch, the guilty pendants — buys the ending its emotion. By the time we reach ‘the snap, / the hinge of rescue’, we have been annoyed enough to feel the relief. The final descent through ‘the exact, / the merciless, / the tender truth’ revises itself twice: clarity is precise, then cruel, then somehow kind. That sequence is the poem’s real subject.

craft.move: Naming the loss as a gain
craft.line: from the wide, beautiful blur
craft.why: One adjective changes the whole poem. If the blur was beautiful, then correction costs something, and the glasses are not simply a rescue. Most poems on this subject never concede it.

craft.line: we hang you from our necks like guilty pendants
craft.why: Guilty of what — needing them? The word smuggles in the shame of ageing that the poem otherwise refuses to state outright.

craft.line: Suddenly, the grain of the paper wakes. / The stubborn footnote speaks. / The old map opens its dry veins.
craft.why: Three sentences, three verbs of animation, escalating from texture to speech to anatomy. The page was alive the whole time; only the eye was absent.

p_d6ca181d49ba9c13.title: Ode to the Mirror
p_d6ca181d49ba9c13.standfirst: A hundred words, an opening oxymoron, and the sharpest final turn in the collection.
paragraphs: ‘You are a cold and honest liar’ sets a contradiction the rest of the poem has to solve. How can something be honest and a liar at once? The answer arrives in the last four lines, and everything between is patient setup.

The middle is the collection’s familiar heading device — ‘The Glass Truth:’, ‘The Daily Theater:’ — but used with more restraint than elsewhere. The three apposed phrases (arbiter, thief, doorway) are compressed rather than expansive, and ‘a doorway where the ego goes to starve’ is the best of them: a door that leads nowhere and a place of fasting in one image.

The close is exact: ‘We ask you, Am I real? / And you always say yes — / right up until / the moment we turn around.’ The mirror’s honesty is entirely conditional on being watched. It is not lying about what it shows; it is lying by ceasing to exist. The poem gets there in eighteen lines with nothing wasted.

craft.move: The whole poem in the first line
craft.line: You are a cold and honest liar.
craft.why: Two contradictory charges laid at once, unexplained. The reader carries the puzzle through the poem, which is why the last line lands as a solution rather than a flourish.

craft.line: You do not judge; you only count / the hours on our skin.
craft.why: The mirror is exonerated and made worse at the same time. Judgement could be argued with; accounting cannot.

craft.line: We arrange ourselves into someone / we might recognize.
craft.why: *Might* is the load-bearing word. The self in the glass is a candidate, not a fact — which is what makes the closing question genuinely frightening.

p_975cd4b601146051.title: Ode to the Refrigerator
p_975cd4b601146051.standfirst: The purest comic ode here — a temple built in three stanzas and demolished by its own last line.
paragraphs: The poem constructs a religion with real care. A ‘humming monolith’ (Kubrick, deadpan), then ‘the Shrine of Illumination’, then ‘the Guardian of Tomorrow’. Each heading escalates. The light becomes revelation, the leftovers become a relic, the appliance becomes a god who holds back decay and the hot chaos of the world.

Then: ‘You only request that I stop / standing there with the door wide open.’ The deity’s single commandment is the thing a parent says. Everything built over sixteen lines collapses into domestic nagging, and the collapse is the point — the sacred and the household are the same place, which is the argument every good comic ode is secretly making.
‘A single bulb judges my life choices’ is the line that carries the poem’s middle. It is funny, and it is also the only moment where the speaker is looked at rather than looking.

craft.move: A punchline that reverses the frame
craft.line: You only request that I stop / standing there with the door wide open.
craft.why: The comic timing depends on withholding it to the final couplet. Placed anywhere earlier, the temple would never have been built.

craft.line: You hold yesterday’s soup like a sacred relic.
craft.why: Relics are body parts of saints kept in gold. Soup in a plastic tub gets the same reverence, and neither term is diminished.

craft.move: Light as revelation and as accusation
craft.line: Night yields to artificial dawn. / A single bulb judges my life choices.
craft.why: Two lines, two opposite uses of the same lamp. The second undercuts the first before the reader has finished admiring it.

p_7f25d7a3a23ac21e.title: Ode to the Id
p_7f25d7a3a23ac21e.standfirst: Freud played for comedy, with a serious defence of appetite hidden in the second stanza.
paragraphs: The characterisation is quick and physical — ‘the ancient tenant of the dark basement’, ‘the messy toddler of the mind’, an absolute monarch who ignores the cholesterol report. The poem is enjoying itself, and the accumulation of domestic detail keeps a psychoanalytic abstraction concrete.

But the poem is not only joking. ‘Without your unfiltered greed, / the human race stops at the first hurdle— / too polite to eat the mammoth, / too polite to kiss the stranger.’ That is a real argument: civilisation is downstream of appetite, and manners alone would have starved us. The threefold repetition of *polite* across the poem turns a virtue into a diagnosis.

‘Stardust / with teeth’ takes a phrase that has been worn smooth by inspirational posters and puts a predator back in it. The line break does the work — *stardust* alone would be sentimental; the teeth arrive after the pause.

craft.line: beneath the polite beige of our manners
craft.why: Beige is the exactly right shade for suppressed appetite — not repressive black, just committee-room blandness. One adjective does what a stanza of argument would.

craft.line: too polite to eat the mammoth, / too polite to kiss the stranger
craft.why: Food and sex, survival and reproduction, in parallel clauses. It is a joke and a serious account of what appetite is for.

craft.line: You see, / you want, / you take—
craft.why: Three lines of two words each, each a stage of desire completing itself. The dash lets the ego arrive to clean up in the next line, exactly as Freud’s model has it.

p_c7043a250623d106.title: Ode to i
p_c7043a250623d106.standfirst: The most conceptual poem here — forty-nine lines on a single letter, using typography to argue about the self.
paragraphs: The conceit is that a lowercase i is a diagram of a person: an upright stem, ‘linear, teetering, / human-like’, and above it a dot that can never be reached. Everything follows from that reading. The stem is life, arrow, time; the dot is whatever is beyond time, ‘approaching, but never touching, / eternally separate.’ Sustaining this for forty-nine lines is the poem’s ambition and its risk.

The insight that saves it from being a clever exercise comes late: ‘both the line and dot are stamped / in the same ink, / on the same paper.’ Transcendence and mortality share a substrate. Whatever the dot represents, it is made of exactly what the stem is made of — and only together do they earn promotion to ‘the Whitmanian, / exulted, upper case I.’

The poem asks a great many questions, and a reader may tire before the answer arrives. It is also worth noticing that the fourth line contains a real exclamation point, so the page performs the ‘astonishing inversion’ the poem is describing at the moment it describes it.

craft.line: the astonishing inversion / of the exclamation point!
craft.why: The punctuation mark appears in the line that names it. The reader sees the inverted i before being told to look for it.

craft.line: But does this lack / indicate shallowness / or does its singularity / imply unseen possibilities?
craft.why: The poem refuses to resolve whether the dot’s dimensionlessness is emptiness or infinity. Holding both is more honest than choosing.

craft.line: to the Whitmanian, / exulted, upper case I
craft.why: Naming Whitman turns a typographic game into a statement about American poetry’s enormous first person — and about the modesty of not yet deserving it.

p_c1c07161cb8a915b.title: Ode to an Ammonite
p_c1c07161cb8a915b.standfirst: Twenty unbroken lines of deep time, containing what may be the single best line in the collection.
paragraphs: The poem opens like an epitaph — ‘You lived. / You swam. / You were buoyant. / You were rapacious.’ Four short declaratives, all past tense, so the death is established before the life is described. Then the geological roll-call: Devonian, Permian, Triassic, Jurassic, Cretaceous. This is a survival story that we already know ends badly, and reading it is like watching someone run out of luck across 360 million years.

‘You slipped through the needle-eye of the Permian’s end— / survivor of the Great Dying—’ gives the creature agency and near-miss drama; the em-dashes hold the reader in the gap the ammonite squeezed through. Then the flat sentence: ‘You and yours perished, extinct.’ No metaphor. The poem stops performing at the moment of loss, which is the correct instinct.

The consolation offered at the end is formal rather than vital. The animal is gone; the shape isn’t. ‘Your form, curled and helical… / endures, circling / against time.’ Since a poem is also a form that outlasts the person who made it, this is quietly about more than a fossil.

craft.move: A pun that is also a fact
craft.line: until the Cretaceous fire turned your ink to stone
craft.why: Ammonites were cephalopods and really did carry ink. The line is simultaneously literal palaeontology and a metaphor for writing petrified into record — the best compression in the collection.

craft.line: like the ram’s horn of Ammon
craft.why: The creature’s name comes from the Egyptian god’s spiral horns. Reaching the etymology at the close makes the naming feel like an arrival rather than a footnote.

craft.line: your various snakestone homes
craft.why: The poem is a single twenty-line spiral with no stanza breaks — one continuous coil, like the shell. ‘Snakestone’ recovers the folk name English quarrymen used before the science existed.

p_42802cc48daa64f2.title: Ode to the American Crow
p_42802cc48daa64f2.standfirst: Field observation used as social satire — the bird is smarter than the commuters, and the poem has the documentation to prove it.
paragraphs: The crow is dressed as a professional throughout: ‘burnished diplomat’, ‘pragmatist / in a suit of oil-slicked velvet’, a philosopher on a telephone wire. What keeps this from being whimsy is that the central example is real behaviour. Crows do drop nuts on crosswalks and wait for traffic to stop. The poem simply reports it — ‘mastering the mechanics of the metropolis / better than the commuters trapped in their metal cages’ — and the satire assembles itself.

‘Trapped in their metal cages’ is the pivot: the caged animal turns out to be the human, and the bird is the one moving freely through the city. The poem’s judgements about accumulation and dividends land because the crow never argues; it just eats better than we do.

The ending refuses to make the crow virtuous. Wisdom here is ‘a stolen silver pendant, / winking in the sun’ — still theft, unrepented, and admired anyway. That is a more interesting moral than the poem could have reached by cleaning the bird up.

craft.line: You crack your stolen walnut on the crosswalk / and wait patiently for the pedestrian light to turn green
craft.why: Documented corvid behaviour, reported without embellishment. The satire needs no exaggeration because the bird really is doing this.

craft.line: in a suit of oil-slicked velvet, / laughing through a throat full of gravel
craft.why: Velvet and gravel in consecutive lines — the crow is elegant to look at and ugly to hear, and the poem likes it for both.

craft.line: intelligence / need not be drunk with solemnity
craft.why: A statement of the collection’s own method. Nearly every poem here treats seriousness and comedy as compatible, and this line says so out loud.

p_9be62ade0df5d1b2.title: Ode to Life
p_9be62ade0df5d1b2.standfirst: The loosest and most personal poem here, running on stand-up rhythm until one stanza stops being funny.
paragraphs: The comic engine is deflation: every grand phrase is immediately undercut by a domestic one. ‘The anatomy of existing’ turns out to mean beating the alarm by four minutes. ‘The Grand Finale of Right Now’ turns out to mean burning toast. The pattern is consistent enough to become the poem’s form.

‘Collecting small, shiny moments / like a raccoon with a Wi-Fi password’ is the funniest line in the collection — absurd, precise, and quietly accurate about how attention actually works. It sits alongside the DNA poem’s burning-building librarian as the two similes that best repay rereading.

Then the 3 a.m. stanza, which is the only place the humour drops out: ‘my brain reviewed / that awkward thing I said last Tuesday.’ It is phrased as another joke but it isn’t one, and the poem is better for letting that show. The ending declines any epiphany — the wind is ‘an acceptable manager for the day’ — which is the real argument: a life is administered, not conquered. (Small housekeeping: there is a stray apostrophe after ‘combustion’.)

craft.line: like a raccoon with a Wi-Fi password
craft.why: Two incompatible registers — wildlife and domestic technology — held together by the idea of small stolen valuables. It is funny first and true second.

craft.line: I decide it is an acceptable manager for the day
craft.why: ‘Acceptable manager’ is the language of a performance review. Applying it to the wind is both a joke and a genuinely modest account of how one gets through a Tuesday.

craft.line: but then accepting the floor tile as my new home
craft.why: The poem does not describe giving up; it describes lying down. Concrete action carries the emotion, which is why it earns its laugh.

p_8a651b789761bc59.title: Ode to Lice
p_8a651b789761bc59.standfirst: The riskiest poem in the collection: a mock-heroic taxonomy in three kingdoms that ends somewhere genuinely sad.
paragraphs: The structure is a field guide crossed with a political map. Three species, three binomials, three social classes — ‘the aristocracy in the attic’ on the head, ‘the phantom of the fibers’ in clothing, ‘the crab of the lowlands’ below. The conceit of lice as a governed order is sustained with real discipline: kingdoms, a republic, a tax collector, a conquistador, a shipwrecked king refusing exile.

The middle section is the best writing. ‘A stowaway in borrowed clothes, / you haunt the lining, seam, and hem, / waiting like a patient pickpocket / for the body to return’ is genuinely unsettling because it is accurate — body lice do live in clothing rather than on skin. Nothing here is invented for effect.

What lifts the poem above its own joke is the last movement. The mock-heroic register holds until ‘the proudest stride / into a suspicious shuffle’, and then drops into ‘public, scratching heartbreak.’ Humiliation, not comedy, is where the poem was going. Choosing a subject this unlovely and finding shame at the bottom of it is the boldest thing in the collection.

craft.line: and the warm republic of unwashed wool
craft.why: Each species gets a form of government matched to its habitat. The metaphor is not decorative — it organises the entire poem, and lets the third section arrive as a fall from office.

craft.line: waiting like a patient pickpocket / for the body to return
craft.why: The line is disturbing because it is true to the biology. The poem never needs to exaggerate; the actual life cycle does the work.

craft.line: until at last, what began in secret / announces itself to the world / as public, scratching heartbreak
craft.why: Forty lines of mock-epic diction give way to one plain, painful noun. The tonal drop is the poem’s real subject: dignity is what is actually being lost.

p_141a8d4382521f25.title: Ode to Water
p_141a8d4382521f25.standfirst: A physics lecture in verse — the longest and most didactic poem here, at its best when it stops explaining and starts compressing.
paragraphs: The poem follows water through its phases, using Celsius and his scale as the organising frame. Its finest moment is also its shortest: ‘solid, liquid, and gas, / which is to say: halt, flow, and soar.’ Three technical terms translated into three verbs of motion — that single line does more than the twenty around it, and shows what the poem can do when it trusts compression.

The governing device is social. Molecules ‘clasp hands with others of their ilk’, are ‘overwhelmed by fleeting attractions’, escape ‘the binding ties / of constant conversation’, and later ‘slow to socialize with compatriots.’ Water is written as a crowd — sometimes imprisoned, sometimes dancing, sometimes conversing. It is a consistent and rather charming way to make thermodynamics feel populated.

Its weakness is length. At 333 words this is nearly twice the collection’s average, and the explanatory impulse sometimes outruns the music — several stanzas would survive losing a third of their lines. The chiasmus at the end (‘the physics of beauty, / or, if you prefer, the beauty of physics’) is a clean way out. (Housekeeping: there is a stray closing quotation mark after the final line.)

craft.line: solid, liquid, and gas, / which is to say: halt, flow, and soar
craft.why: The three states become three verbs, and the abstraction turns kinetic. The rest of the poem takes sixty lines to say what this line says in two.

craft.line: interlocking into the cells / of a frozen hexagonal prison
craft.why: ‘Cells’ is doing double work — crystal lattice and jail. The pun sets up ‘liquid liberty’ later, so the whole poem runs on a politics of freedom and constraint.

craft.line: Catch them in your gloved hand: / each flake unique. / You’ve just received nature’s invitation
craft.why: After sixty lines of third-person physics the poem finally addresses the reader and asks them to put a hand out. The shift to second person is where the lecture becomes an ode.

p_58ed4884eb0ef37e.title: Ode to Breath as Prayer
p_58ed4884eb0ef37e.standfirst: A cathedral built and then cheerfully refused — the most materialist poem here, and one of the funniest.
paragraphs: The opening establishes the method in three lines: ‘In the cathedral of the quiet lung, no organ plays. / The choir is just a diaphragm, / rising like a stubborn sourdough.’ Cathedral, then immediately bread dough. Every sacred term in this poem is punctured by a kitchen one, and the puncturing is affectionate rather than mocking.

The physiology is exact. The intercostals really are what you bow with; the pause between inhalation and exhalation really is a distinct phase; the poem’s ‘Liturgy of Inhalation’ and ‘Confession of Exhalation’ map onto a real respiratory cycle. That accuracy is what lets the comedy sit on top without collapsing.

The ending refuses transcendence outright: ‘No one is listening on the other side of the ribs.’ There is no god in this cathedral, only a body keeping its own score — and the poem decides that is sufficient. ‘The best religion / is the one that keeps you from turning blue’ is a joke that also states a materialist creed, and it lands because the poem has been reverent for thirty lines first.

craft.line: The choir is just a diaphragm, / rising like a stubborn sourdough
craft.why: The cathedral survives exactly one line before the bread arrives. Establishing the pattern this early tells the reader how to read everything that follows.

craft.line: tasting of old asphalt, burnt coffee, / and the electric smell of rain before it hits the dust
craft.why: Petrichor named without the word. The third item is the only one that anticipates rather than remembers, which quietly makes inhalation about the future.

craft.line: It is the only true blank page / the nervous system ever gets
craft.why: The pause after exhalation is reframed as rest rather than absence. For a poem about breathing, locating the peace in the empty half is a genuine observation.

p_6bfe3257d0ab3a87.title: Ode to Carbon
p_6bfe3257d0ab3a87.standfirst: The poem enacts its own subject — it travels the carbon cycle, from star to diamond to toast to us and back into the rock.
paragraphs: The chemistry here is not ornament. ‘The promiscuous binder of all that is real’ is a precise description of tetravalence and a moral judgement in the same phrase; ‘four open hands reaching out for partners, / eager to touch and to share a lasting valence’ turns bonding into affection without falsifying anything. Carbon is sociable because carbon genuinely is.

‘Ringing in sixes that smell of old gasoline’ is the most compressed line — benzene rings, and benzene really does smell like that. A reader who knows the chemistry gets a fact; a reader who doesn’t gets a filling station on a summer afternoon. Both readings are correct, which is the best kind of technical image.

The structure is the argument. The poem moves from ‘cold, lonely stretches of space’ through diamond, through burnt toast, through us ‘as we worry, as we swallow our sugar’, and then ‘sinking back down into quiet strata.’ The poem is shaped like the cycle it describes, so the ending arrives where the beginning was.

craft.line: the promiscuous binder of all that is real
craft.why: One adjective covers valence, ubiquity and appetite. It is scientifically exact and slightly scandalous, which is the tone the whole poem wants.

craft.move: Cosmic to domestic in one line
craft.line: Flaking from edges of burnt morning toast / like confetti of black
craft.why: After stars and diamonds, breakfast. ‘Confetti’ adds celebration to what is only carbonised bread — the poem keeps insisting that the humble instance is the same substance as the grand one.

craft.move: The reader placed inside the cycle
craft.line: Walking around on two legs as we talk, / as we worry, as we swallow our sugar.
craft.why: The apostrophe briefly turns: for three lines, the thing being addressed is us. We are what carbon is currently doing.

p_7faac0490d8c3943.title: Ode to a Solar Eclipse
p_7faac0490d8c3943.standfirst: An erotic conceit that swerves, mid-poem, into something maternal — and a crowd who need smoked glass to watch.
paragraphs: The poem is frank about what it is doing. Sun and moon are ‘public lovers’; the poem asks outright ‘who is doing the mounting?’; the crowd gathers to watch two bodies touch ‘after such lengthy correspondence.’ The opening line about the smoked glass — ‘the practicality of censorship’ — is the cleverest thing here: the filter genuinely protects the retina, and simultaneously makes the watching furtive, as though the spectacle needed covering.

The two bodies are characterised as opposites in medium. The sun is sound and motion — ‘a brass section, / all trumpets and trombones.’ The moon is stone and silence — ‘a chiseled likeness / without light of its own: / a marbled echo, / a statue of Apollo.’ Noise against sculpture is an unusual pairing for an eclipse and it keeps the poem from the usual imagery of shadow and disc.

Then the swerve. Having built the erotic reading carefully, the poem reaches the moment of contact and offers instead ‘a mother’s palm / on a child’s feverish forehead.’ Cooling, not consummation. It is a real reversal, and it is generous — the poem decides at the last moment that this is care rather than conquest. The crow cawing thrice at the close is a nice touch of false evening, and links the poem to the crow ode elsewhere in the collection.

craft.move: A phrase that does two jobs
craft.line: to gaze through smoked glass: / the practicality of censorship
craft.why: Eye protection and prudery in the same image. It establishes the poem’s erotic frame before a single body has moved.

craft.move: Domestic simile for a cosmic event
craft.line: like hot and cold handles / on the faucet
craft.why: The sun and moon reduced to bathroom fittings — which is exactly how we experience opposites daily. It grounds the poem before it becomes grand.

craft.line: as a mother’s palm / on a child’s feverish forehead
craft.why: The poem abandons its own conceit at the climax and substitutes tenderness. Whether or not this was planned, it is the most humane moment in the collection.

p_aa2c871b5b13f7b9.title: Ode to the Double-Crested Cormorant
p_aa2c871b5b13f7b9.standfirst: The most patient watching here — a poem that asks a question about a bird’s posture and honourably refuses to answer it.
paragraphs: The poem is organised around etymology. Phalacrocorax is Greek for bald raven; auritus means horned, which explains the breeding crests. Working outward from the name is a method this collection uses often, but nowhere more thoroughly — the taxonomy generates the description rather than decorating it.

Its intelligence is in the unanswered question. The cormorant’s spread-wing pose is offered two readings: ‘Is it a gesture, / or simply to dry the feathers’ — ritual or plumbing. The poem then extends the ambiguity into ‘this posture like an orator, / limbs uplifted, about to speak, / but never to go beyond, / as if to mock?’ and leaves it open. Ornithologists genuinely disagree about this behaviour; the poem’s refusal to settle it is a form of accuracy.

The ending declines every elegance the poem has earned. After the sphinx, the orator and the aquamarine eyes, we arrive at ‘gaping mouths’ and ‘garbled, guttural grunts’ — three hard g sounds in a row, deliberately unlovely. The bird is beautiful at rest and grotesque while feeding its young, and the poem insists on showing both.

craft.line: Is it a gesture, / or simply to dry the feathers
craft.why: A lesser poem would choose. Keeping both readings alive is more truthful to the bird and lets the sphinx comparison stand for the whole species.

craft.move: The neck as the poem’s spine
craft.line: or swimming low in the water, / the supple neck gone snake-like
craft.why: The neck recurs four times — folded, snake-like, elongated, caressing — and each posture tells you what the bird is doing. It is the poem’s unit of observation.

craft.line: with garbled, guttural grunts
craft.why: The alliteration is harsh where the rest of the poem is fluid. Ending on the noise of regurgitation refuses to leave the reader with an elegant bird.

p_84b827ff7adcbae9.title: Ode to DNA
p_84b827ff7adcbae9.standfirst: An ode to something entirely indifferent to us, containing the best simile in the collection and a list that justifies the whole poem.
paragraphs: The poem’s move is to refuse the usual awe. DNA here is ‘the ultimate egoist’ that does not care about the sky, the thrush, or our keys. It wants one thing, forever. That flat, slightly comic indifference is more interesting than reverence would have been, and it sets up the turn.

‘Like a very stubborn librarian / stuck in a burning building / who saves the alphabet first’ is the finest simile here. It is funny, it is exactly right about what replication prioritises, and the word *alphabet* is doing quiet double duty — the four bases really are a writing system.

Then the poem earns its ending. Out of ‘this microscopic stutter’ comes ‘the taste of cold salt water, / the terror of a Tuesday, / and the way a hand looks / in the light of a kitchen lamp.’ Sensation, dread, and a domestic image of someone you love — three scales in three lines. That list is the argument: the indifferent code produces everything that matters, and none of it was the point. ‘We are your clumsy footnotes’ follows naturally, and the closing image of pages turning after we are gone is the collection’s most unsentimental consolation.

craft.line: You are the ultimate egoist.
craft.why: Molecules are usually made noble in poems. Making this one selfish and a little tiresome is funnier and, in evolutionary terms, more accurate.

craft.line: of Adenine, Thymine, Cytosine, and Guanine— / four monks chanting in a row
craft.why: Four long polysyllables read aloud do sound like plainsong. The simile is derived from the sound of the words themselves, not imposed on them.

craft.move: A list that changes scale each line
craft.line: the terror of a Tuesday, / and the way a hand looks / in the light of a kitchen lamp
craft.why: From physical sensation to existential dread to one specific person’s hand. The narrowing focus is what makes the abstraction land emotionally.
